case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course. This case highlights the diagnostic complexities of PS-DLBCL stemming from initial nonspecific radiographic findings and hyperinflammatory symptoms, along with potential iatrogenic complications with a delay in diagnosis. A high degree of clinical suspicion is required to ensure clinicians consider this rare diagnosis when evaluating a patient with splenomegaly and persistent fevers.

case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course.
